qs.q: A patient with suspected acute leukaemia undergoes diagnostic workup. What minimum percentage of blasts in the bone marrow or peripheral blood is required by WHO criteria to confirm a diagnosis of acute leukaemia?
o: A. Greater than or equal to 10% blasts
B. Greater than or equal to 20% blasts
C. Greater than or equal to 30% blasts
D. Greater than or equal to 50% blasts
qs.e: The WHO diagnostic criterion for acute leukaemia requires the presence of 20% or more blasts in either the bone marrow or peripheral blood. Lower percentages of blasts are insufficient for this classification.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: When performing cytochemical staining to confirm the myeloid lineage of blasts in a patient with acute leukaemia, which stain is considered the most specific for myeloid cells?
qs.e: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is the most specific cytochemical stain for confirming myeloid lineage in acute leukaemia. Periodic acid-Schiff is more typically associated with lymphoid or erythroid lineage confirmation.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A peripheral blood film from an adult patient with acute leukaemia reveals prominent pink needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions within the malignant myeloid blasts. What is the name of these characteristic structures?
qs.e: Auer rods are a diagnostic hallmark seen in acute myeloid leukaemia blasts. Smear cells are associated with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, and Reed-Sternberg cells are found in Hodgkin lymphoma.
